Yorktown. In September and October of 1781, American and French forces under George Washington surrounded British General Lord Cornwallis at Yorktown, Virginia. Cornwallis had retreated to Yorktown with roughly 7,000 men, but Washington and French General Comte de Rochambeau converged with approximately 17,000 troops and artillery. The French Navy's victory at the Battle of the Capes prevented British reinforcement or evacuation by sea. Trapped between American infantry, French ships blocking escape by water, and no hope of relief, Cornwallis surrendered on October 19, 1781. American and French artillery bombarded the British defenses, and the Allies captured a series of outer fortifications. Cornwallis surrendered approximately 7,000 soldiers—the largest British capitulation of the war and a decisive blow to Britain's ability to continue fighting. British losses and the scale of surrender shocked Parliament, and peace negotiations began within months. Yorktown effectively sealed the British defeat and led to the Treaty of Paris in 1783, which granted American independence. The victory was as much a French triumph—Rochambeau's army, the naval blockade—as an American one, cementing the Franco-American alliance.
